title: Hezekiah's Passover: An Invitation to All Israel
summary: Hezekiah sends couriers from Beersheba to Dan inviting the whole people, including the survivors of the northern tribes, to keep the Passover in Jerusalem. Many in the north mock the messengers, but some humble themselves and come. The feast is held a month late, some worshipers eat without being ritually purified, and Hezekiah prays for their pardon; the LORD hears and heals the people, and the celebration is extended to fourteen days with joy unmatched since Solomon.
story: With the temple cleansed in chapter 29, Hezekiah turns to the people. Since the kingdom divided after Solomon's death, the northern tribes had worshiped apart from Jerusalem, and many had now been deported by Assyria. Hezekiah's letters are an attempt to gather what remains of all Israel around the one house of God. This is the Chronicler's great hope on display: not Judah alone, but the twelve tribes reunited in worship. The chapter also shows grace outrunning procedure, as God accepts seekers who come imperfectly prepared. The reform will continue in chapter 31 as the joy of the feast spills out into the destruction of idols across the land.
historical:
The invitation addresses those “who have escaped the grasp of the kings of Assyria” (verse 6), which places the event after Assyria's campaigns against the northern kingdom: Tiglath-pileser III deported people from Galilee and Gilead around 732 BC, and Samaria fell in 722 BC. If Hezekiah's reign began around 715 BC, the northern kingdom no longer existed, and the invitation went to a scattered remnant living under Assyrian provincial rule. If it began around 727 BC, the event might fall just before or after Samaria's fall. Either way, sending couriers into Assyrian-controlled territory was a bold act.

2 Kings does not mention this Passover, and 2 Kings 23:22 says of Josiah's later Passover that none like it had been kept since the days of the judges. Interpreters explain this in various ways: Kings may mean that Josiah's Passover was unmatched in its strict conformity to the book of the law, while Hezekiah's was irregular; or the Chronicler may be drawing on sources Kings did not use. Some scholars think the Chronicler has shaped this account to present Hezekiah as a new Solomon. The comparison with Solomon in verse 26 fits that emphasis.
cultural:
Passover commemorated Israel's deliverance from Egypt (Exodus 12) and was to be kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, followed by the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread. The Law allowed a person who was unclean or on a distant trip to keep it a month later (Numbers 9:9-11). Hezekiah applies that provision to the whole nation, since the priests were not ready and the people had not gathered in time.

Ritual purity mattered because contact with death, certain illnesses, and other conditions made a person unfit to eat holy food until cleansed. Many northerners had no experience of these rules after two centuries of separate worship, so the Levites slaughtered lambs on their behalf (verse 17). Destroying the altars and incense altars of Jerusalem and throwing them into the Kidron Valley (verse 14) completed the cleansing Ahaz's idolatry had made necessary. Letters carried by royal couriers were the ordinary means of state communication in this period, and the king's letter here is written as a prophetic sermon.
literary: Hezekiah's letter (verses 6-9) is built on the Hebrew verb shuv, to return, which appears again and again: return to the LORD so that he may return to you; if you return, your captives will return; he will not turn his face from you if you return. The letter echoes Exodus 34:6 in calling the LORD gracious and merciful. The couriers' reception is mixed: mockery in verse 10, humility in verse 11, and in Judah a heart made one by the power of God (verse 12). The chapter ends with two prayers answered. Hezekiah prays for the unclean and “the LORD heard” (verse 20); the priests bless the people and “God heard their voice” (verse 27). The comparison with Solomon's day in verse 26 recalls Solomon's dedication prayer in chapter 6, where he asked God to hear from heaven, his dwelling place.

outline.t: The decision to keep Passover in the second month
The king's letter: return to the LORD
Mockery in the north, humility in some, unity in Judah
Altars removed and the Passover lambs slaughtered
Hezekiah's prayer for the unclean and the LORD's healing
Fourteen days of feasting and a blessing heard in heaven

doctrines.note: The call to return is the heart of the chapter. Repentance is pictured as a two-way turning: when the people return to God, he returns to them, because he is gracious and merciful.

Hezekiah intercedes for people who have broken the purity rules, and the LORD hears and heals. The priests' blessing also reaches God's holy dwelling in heaven. Prayer here is effective because God has promised to hear.
The feast gathers Judah, the northern tribes, and even resident foreigners into one rejoicing assembly. The unity of God's people is shown as worship around one altar, not merely political alliance.

words.note: Shuv, to turn or return. It is the Old Testament's main word for repentance, and it can also describe a return from exile. The letter plays on both senses: if the people turn back to God, their captives may return to the land.
Channun, gracious. With rachum, merciful, it recalls God's self-description to Moses in Exodus 34:6. The king grounds his invitation not in Israel's merit but in the character of God.

Rapha, to heal. In verse 20 the LORD heals the people, which may mean sparing them from the sickness that impurity could bring, or more broadly restoring them. It recalls God's promise in 7:14 to heal the land of a people who humble themselves and pray.

Levav, heart. Hezekiah asks pardon for everyone who sets his heart on seeking God, even if not cleansed by the rules (verse 19). The heart's direction is put ahead of ritual correctness, without dismissing the rules themselves.

christ: Passover is the feast the New Testament connects most directly to Christ. Jesus died at Passover, and Paul writes, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Hezekiah's Passover adds its own shading. It is an invitation sent to the scattered and the scornful, calling them home to the house of God; the Gospels describe Jesus gathering the lost sheep of Israel and then sending his followers to all nations. It welcomes worshipers who were not properly prepared, on the strength of a king's prayer; the New Testament presents Jesus as the king who intercedes for his people (Hebrews 7:25). These links are thematic, not predictions within Chronicles, but they show why this chapter has spoken to Christians about grace.

hard.q: If God gave detailed purity laws, why does he accept people who broke them here?
hard.a: The text itself admits the irregularity: the people ate “contrary to what was written” (verse 18). Hezekiah does not pretend the rules don't matter; he asks God to pardon those who seek him with their heart. The LORD's answer shows that the law served the relationship rather than replacing it, a theme the prophets also press (Hosea 6:6). Some interpreters stress that this was an exceptional act of mercy in an emergency, not a new rule, and that the priests and Levites themselves made sure the sacrifices were still properly handled. Others see it as an early instance of the principle that God looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). Both readings keep the tension the text preserves: the rules are real, and God's grace is greater.

questions: Hezekiah's couriers were mocked by many but welcomed by some. How do you respond when an invitation to return to God is received with scorn?
God accepted people whose hearts were set on seeking him even though they were not ritually prepared. How does that shape the way you welcome newcomers to worship?
The assembly chose to extend the feast for seven more days. When have you experienced worship or fellowship you did not want to end, and what made it so?
